# Respondents {#sec-respondents}

The quantities in the earlier chapters describe the population. This chapter turns to individual
respondents: what the fitted model says about one respondent's tastes, given that respondent's
characteristics and choices. `sc_posterior()` computes it.

```{r}
#| label: r-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
```

## What a posterior is here

Before we see any choices, the model predicts a respondent's tastes from their characteristics:
the tastes are normal, with mean $\mu(Z_i)$ and covariance $\Lambda\Lambda^\top$. This is the
*prior*. Each observed choice is more likely under some tastes than others. Bayes' rule combines the
prior with the choices into the *posterior*: an updated distribution of that
respondent's tastes, at the fitted parameters.

With thirteen tasks, the choices tell us only a little. The posterior then stays close to the
prior, and the posterior mean is pulled toward the mean of respondents with the same
characteristics. It is a prediction of the respondent's tastes, not a measurement of them. Only with
many tasks does the posterior concentrate around the respondent's own tastes.

## A few partisans in the democracy experiment

For fold states, `sc_posterior()` uses each respondent's held-out fit: the one that did not train
on their choices. A contrast is given as a named vector or a matrix with one row per contrast.

```{r}
#| label: r-gs
partisans <- which(gs$data$groups$PL == 1)
cp <- matrix(1, 1, 1, dimnames = list("co-partisan", "diff_respParty"))
post <- sc_posterior(gs, respondents = partisans[1:6], contrasts = cp)
post
round(post$contrasts[, c("prior_mean", "prior_sd", "mean", "sd", "lower", "upper",
                         "prob_positive")], 2)
```

The first two respondents had similar priors, a co-partisan taste of about 1.4 and 1.1 with a
standard deviation of 0.87. After their thirteen choices, the first respondent's posterior mean
rises to 1.75 and the second's falls to 0.27. `prob_positive` is the posterior probability that
the respondent's co-partisan taste is positive. The posterior standard deviations are about three
quarters of the prior ones. `history = 0` returns the prior itself:

```{r}
#| label: r-history0
round(sc_posterior(gs, respondents = partisans[1:2], contrasts = cp, history = 0)$contrasts[,
  c("prior_mean", "mean", "sd")], 2)
```

## Do not count posterior means

It is tempting to summarize the population by counting respondents whose posterior mean is
positive. That is not an estimate of the preference share. Posterior means are shrunk toward the
prior means, so their spread is smaller than the spread of tastes, and their signs follow the
prior. The population quantities of the earlier chapters average over each respondent's whole taste
distribution instead.

```{r}
#| label: r-count
all_pl <- sc_posterior(gs, respondents = partisans, contrasts = cp)
law <- sc_fitted_law(gs, "diff_respParty", w = "PL")
rbind(
  "posterior means" = c(sd = sd(all_pl$contrasts$mean), positive = mean(all_pl$contrasts$mean > 0)),
  "fitted law" = c(sd = attr(law, "summary")[["sd"]], positive = attr(law, "summary")[["share_positive"]]))
```

The spread of the 1,377 posterior means is smaller than the spread of the fitted law. The share
with a positive posterior mean is also not the fitted share of 83.3%, nor the corrected share of
82.5% in @sec-gs. The posterior summaries also condition on the fitted parameters, so they carry
no sampling uncertainty from the fit.

## Long panels: a simulated example

With many tasks per respondent the posterior can learn individual tastes. The paper shows this
with a 30-task experiment. Here we simulate one with known tastes: 200 respondents, 30 tasks each,
three coded features, one taste factor and a position effect. `sc_posterior()` also takes fitted
parameters directly, as a list with `mu`, `kappa`, `loading` and `omega`.

```{r}
#| label: r-sim
set.seed(30)
n <- 200; n_tasks <- 30; p <- 3
X <- matrix(sample(c(-1, 0, 1), n * n_tasks * p, TRUE), n * n_tasks, p,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("party", "college", "experience")))
id <- rep(seq_len(n), each = n_tasks)
mu <- cbind(party = rnorm(n, 0.8, 0.3), college = rnorm(n, 0.3, 0.2), experience = 0.2)
L <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.4, 0.2), p, 1)
beta <- mu + rnorm(n) %o% L[, 1]
omega <- 0.3; kappa <- 0.1
y <- rbinom(n * n_tasks, 1, plogis(kappa + rowSums(X * beta[id, ]) + sqrt(omega) * rnorm(n)[id]))
dat <- sc_data(y, X, id)
par_true <- list(mu = mu, kappa = kappa, loading = L, omega = omega)
```

For each history (the number of each respondent's first tasks conditioned on), we compute the
posterior of the party taste and predict the final five tasks. The parameters are the true ones,
so the table shows what the choices themselves add.

```{r}
#| label: r-learning
learn <- t(sapply(c(0, 3, 8, 15, 25), function(h) {
  newtasks <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) X[id == i, , drop = FALSE][26:30, ])
  post <- sc_posterior(par_true, dat, contrasts = c(party = 1), history = h, newtasks = newtasks)
  obs <- y[rep(seq_len(n_tasks), n) > 25]
  pr <- post$predictions$prob
  c(history = h,
    posterior_sd = median(post$contrasts$sd),
    cor_with_truth = cor(post$contrasts$mean, beta[, "party"]),
    log_loss_last5 = -mean(obs * log(pr) + (1 - obs) * log(1 - pr)))
}))
round(learn, 3)
```

As the history grows, the posterior standard deviation of the party taste falls, the posterior
means track the true tastes more closely, and the predictions of the last five choices improve.
With 25 earlier choices the posterior is still far from a point: respondents' choices are noisy,
and each task carries little information about any one taste.

The default integrator (`method = "adaptive"`) centers its draws at each respondent's posterior
mode, so it stays accurate when the posterior is much narrower than the prior. The `diagnostics`
table reports each respondent's effective sample size; a small value means the draws should be
increased with `nodes`.
